analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority to regulate how cigarettes are made, marketed, and sold.
analysis.headline: The bill that would have let the FDA regulate cigarettes for the first time died in a Senate committee without ever getting a vote, despite 16 cosponsors split evenly between both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made the FDA the federal regulator of tobacco for the first time. Cigarette makers would have to register their factories, disclose their ingredients, submit to inspections, pay fees, and get approval before selling new products or making health claims. It banned flavored cigarettes (except menthol), let the FDA restrict tobacco advertising that reaches young people, and let the agency recall dangerously defective products. The bill's own findings called tobacco the leading preventable cause of death in America, killing over 400,000 people a year, and said tobacco companies spent more than $11 billion in 2001 alone on marketing that draws in children. It never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate health committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who the bill's findings say are the target of more than $11 billion a year in tobacco marketing; current smokers, who would get accurate ingredient disclosure, honest warning labels, and protection from unproven "less harmful" claims; and everyone exposed to secondhand smoke and tobacco-related health care costs. Adult smokers keep legal access to cigarettes — the bill caps the purchase age at 18 and forbids prescription-only or outlet bans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, teens, smokers, and public health

how_it_helps.text: Gave the FDA power to regulate how tobacco products are made, marketed, and sold — including ingredient disclosure, annual registration, inspection of factories, and user fees — for the first time [S2].

Banned flavored cigarettes designed to attract new, young smokers — strawberry, grape, clove, cinnamon, chocolate, and others [S3] [S2] — and let the FDA restrict advertising and promotion aimed at youth [S2].

Required premarket approval of all new tobacco products and prior review of any claim that a product is less harmful, to stop unproven 'light' and 'low-tar' style claims that the bill's findings said had misled smokers into not quitting [S2] [S3].

The bill's own findings estimated that cutting youth smoking in half would keep more than 6.5 million of today's children from becoming regular smokers, save over 2 million of them from premature death, and save roughly $75 billion in health care costs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers bear the direct cost: registration, inspections, ingredient and health-research disclosure, user fees, and premarket approval of new products. Retailers face advertising and promotion restrictions, though the bill shields face-to-face sales. Some costs would likely reach smokers through prices.

drawbacks.text: The draft contained major carve-outs: menthol was exempt from the flavor ban even though strawberry, clove, cinnamon, cocoa, and every other characterizing flavor were prohibited [S2] [S3].

The bill capped the minimum purchase age at 18, barred the FDA from restricting face-to-face sales by any category of retailer, and expressly reserved to Congress — not the FDA — the power to ban any tobacco product or reduce nicotine to zero [S2].

Tobacco growers and the raw leaf trade were explicitly placed outside the FDA's authority; inspectors could not enter a farm without written consent, leaving the start of the supply chain unregulated [S3].

The bill was to be funded by user fees on tobacco manufacturers [S2], a cost that would tend to be passed on to smokers in prices, and the registration, ingredient-disclosure, and premarket-approval apparatus burdened manufacturers — a cost larger companies are better positioned to absorb than small ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health upside was large: tobacco kills over 400,000 Americans a year, and the bill's own findings estimated that cutting youth smoking in half would keep more than 6.5 million of today's children from becoming regular smokers and save about $75 billion in health care costs [S3]. Against that, the bill had real design flaws an honest supporter would acknowledge: the menthol exemption left the flavor most used by Black smokers untouched [S2], the legal purchase age was capped at 18 [S2], the FDA could not ban a product or reduce nicotine to zero without a new act of Congress [S2], tobacco farming was put beyond FDA reach [S3], and compliance costs were to be recovered from the industry in fees likely passed on to smokers [S2]. Even a strong version, in other words, would have regulated tobacco far more gently than the FDA regulates any other consumable drug. Still, the costs are small next to the deaths at stake, and the bill never got far enough for any of them to matter.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the Senate health committee, and never heard from again; the committee never voted on it and the Senate never debated it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike DeWine introduced S. 2461 on May 20, 2004, with Sen. Edward Kennedy, and it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S1] [S5].
Sixteen senators signed on as cosponsors, eight Democrats and eight Republicans, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship [S4].
The action history shows no markup, no vote, and no further action of any kind after the referral — the bill sat in committee until the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: they kept selling and marketing cigarettes with no federal regulator overseeing ingredients, marketing to children, or health claims, exactly as before. Health groups and the bill's sponsors got nothing.

for.name: Mike DeWine
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S1] [S5].

for.name: Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill with DeWine; the bill text lists DeWine introducing it 'for himself and Mr. Kennedy' [S3].

for.name: 8 of 100 senators (8 Republicans, 8 Democrats cosponsoring)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, split evenly between the two parties [S4].

against.name: Judd Gregg
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee: the record shows no markup, no vote, and no committee action of any kind after the May 2004 referral, through the end of the Congress [S5].

against.name: R.J. Reynolds and other major tobacco companies (excluding Philip Morris)
against.what_they_did: Opposed giving the FDA authority over tobacco products and campaigned against FDA tobacco legislation during this period; Philip Morris, by contrast, supported FDA oversight that would lock in rules favoring large incumbent brands.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly bipartisan — 8 Democratic and 8 Republican cosponsors behind a Republican lead sponsor — but the bill never reached a vote, so the record shows no partisan breakdown on any roll call [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have imposed registration, inspections, ingredient disclosure, user fees, and premarket approval for new products [S2]. But it also grandfathered existing brands, restricted advertising (which favors large incumbent brands with locked-in recognition), and carved out menthol [S2] — protections that weigh hardest on small and newer competitors.

The bill explicitly exempted tobacco leaf, growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives from FDA authority, and barred inspectors from entering a tobacco farm without the owner's written consent [S3].

Retailers faced new restrictions on advertising, promotion, and access — but the bill barred the FDA from prohibiting face-to-face sales by any category of retail outlet, protecting convenience stores and other retailers' core business [S2].

industries.industry: Health insurers and public health programs
industries.note: Reduced smoking means lower treatment costs; the bill's findings cited roughly $75 billion in potential health care savings from halving youth smoking [S3].
